newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan admits nuclear accident cover-up.
newsitem.headline: Japan admits nuclear accident cover-up.

text.p: Supporters and opponents of nuclear power united in anger with government officials on Wednesday after another embarrassing incident forced the shutdown of a power plant.

The beleaguered state-run firm, the Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corp (PNC), was ordered to halt operations at its Fugen reactor in western Japan after it emerged that it had waited 30 hours before reporting a radiation leak that occurred on Monday.
Local government officials in Fukui Prefecture said 11 workers were exposed to small doses of radiation in Monday's accident.
"The amount of radiation the workers were exposed to was within permissible limits," one official said.

The incident was seized upon by nuclear power opponents, who question the government's plan to boost dependency on atomic plants to 42 percent of total capacity by 2010. Japan has virtually no oil or natural gas to provide electric power.
The PNC already faces legal action over its cover-up of key details of an accident last month at a nuclear fuel reprocessing plant northeast of Tokyo.
In what has become a ritual for the company, it admitted it had erred and apologised. It shut down the plant on Tuesday night.
"Our report was delayed because of our misjudgment. I am sorry for causing trouble," Norito Takeshita, head of the Fugen plant, told a news conference on Tuesday.
A PNC spokesman told Reuters technicians dealing with the leak at the advanced thermal reactor in Tsuruga, Fukui Prefecture "relaxed" instead of reporting the problem.
"The report to authorities was delayed partly because the workers were so relieved once they found the cause of the problem," the spokesman said.
But the official explanations did little to cool down Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who said he was disgusted by the incident.
"I saw the date of the accident and the date the PNC reported. It's completely hopeless!" he told reporters.
Last week he blasted the PNC for cover-ups in its report on the fire at the nuclear reprocessing plant, saying the revelations made him speechless.
Top government spokesman Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference the state-run body "should be dismantled and start again from scratch..."
Kajiyama's comments echoed those of the head of the Citizens Nuclear Information Centre, Japan's largest anti-nuclear organisation.
"Let's say 'sayonara' to the PNC. Now, instead of saying 'clean up your act' we should be telling the firm to 'please go away'," said Jinzaburo Takagi, head of the centre.
Fukui prefectural officials said an alarm went off early on Monday after a high level of the radioactive material tritium was detected in a facility in what is Japan's only heavy water reactor.
Later on Wednesday, the Science and Technology Agency, which oversees Japan's nuclear power programme, said they filed a complaint with police against the PNC and several company officials.

The complaint, which would initiate legal action against the PNC or its officials, concerns inaccuracies in a report on the March 11 fire and explosion at the reprocessing plant, which exposed 37 workers to low levels of radiation.

The PNC admitted last week that the report was deliberately altered to suggest falsely that plant workers had checked to ensure that the fire had been doused. The fire flared up later, triggering the explosion.
It was hardly the first time the PNC has been in trouble.

In December 1995, PNC officials admitted they had lied about inspections and tried to suppress videotape footage of a coolant leak at an experimental fast-breeder reactor at Monju, not far from the site of Monday's leakage.

"The recent series of accidents has caused the public to become suspicious about the whole of Japan's nuclear industry," said Kazuya Fujime, managing director of the Institute of Energy Economics, a private think-tank.
